title: How to Make a Fresh Herb Butter Blend Quickly
meta_description: Learn how to make herb butter in minutes. Discover the best herb combinations and a time-saving tool to mince fresh greens for a gourmet finish.
html:
There is something about a dollop of compound butter that transforms a boring piece of grilled protein into a restaurant-quality meal. Whether it is melting over a seared ribeye, swirling into steamed carrots, or spreading across a warm baguette, herb butter adds depth and richness that plain butter simply can't match.

If you have ever avoided making your own because the chopping feels tedious, you aren't alone. Most of us don't want to spend twenty minutes meticulously dicing parsley and chives only to eat them in five. Learning how to make herb butter quickly is all about prepping your ingredients efficiently and choosing the right fat base.

Choosing the Right Butter and Herbs

Start with high-quality unsalted butter. Using unsalted allows you to control the sodium levels, which is important because many of the additives we mix in—like parmesan or garlic—already carry a salty punch. Let your butter sit at room temperature for about an hour until it is soft enough to blend easily with a fork or spatula, but not melted. If you microwave it, you risk breaking the emulsion, which leads to a greasy texture.

For the herbs, stick to what is in season. Flat-leaf parsley and chives are the gold standard for a general-purpose butter. If you want something more Mediterranean, go with basil and oregano. For a woody, earthy vibe—perfect for roasted potatoes—reach for rosemary and thyme. The key is to ensure your herbs are completely dry after washing; excess water can cause the butter to separate or spoil faster in the fridge.

The Secret to Fast Prepping: Herb Scissors

The most time-consuming part of the process is the chopping. Traditional knife work requires a stable cutting board and a lot of repetitive motion to get the herbs fine enough to blend into the butter. To speed this up, I use Herb Scissors. These five-blade herb shears allow you to mince cilantro, chives, and basil in one snip, effectively quintupling your speed.

Instead of gathering herbs into a pile on a board, you can snip them directly into your mixing bowl. This eliminates the transfer step and keeps your workspace clean. Plus, the included cleaning comb makes it easy to remove the stubborn bits of greenery that get stuck between the blades, which is usually the biggest pain point with multi-blade shears.

Step-by-Step: How to Make Herb Butter

Now that your butter is softened and your herbs are prepped, the assembly is the easiest part. Follow these steps for a consistent blend:

  • Soften: Place 1/2 cup of unsalted butter in a medium mixing bowl.
  • Mince: Use your Herb Scissors to chop 2 tablespoons of fresh herbs (parsley, chives, or a mix) directly into the bowl.
  • Season: Add a pinch of kosher salt, a crack of black pepper, and optional additions like one clove of minced garlic or a teaspoon of lemon zest.
  • Blend: Use a fork or a small whisk to fold the ingredients together until the herbs are evenly distributed.
  • Shape: Spoon the mixture onto a piece of parchment paper, roll it into a log, and twist the ends to seal it.

Customizing Your Herb Butter Blends

Once you master the basic technique of how to make herb butter, you can start experimenting with flavor profiles tailored to specific dishes. The beauty of compound butter is its versatility.

For a "Steakhouse Blend," use a combination of garlic, rosemary, and thyme. The earthiness of the rosemary cuts through the richness of the beef. For a "Summer Seafood Blend," try lemon zest, dill, and chives. This is incredible on grilled shrimp or baked cod. If you want a punchy "Tuscan Blend," combine sun-dried tomato bits, basil, and a hint of parmesan cheese.

Storing and Using Your Butter

Stored in the refrigerator, herb butter will stay fresh for about two weeks. However, the best way to preserve it for the long term is in the freezer. Since you’ve already rolled your butter into a parchment log, you can simply slice off a "coin" of butter whenever you need it.

To use it, don't melt the butter in the pan over high heat, as the fresh herbs can burn and become bitter. Instead, place a cold slice of herb butter directly on top of your hot food immediately after removing it from the heat. The residual warmth will melt the butter slowly, creating a rich, aromatic glaze that coats the food perfectly.

FAQ

Can I use dried herbs instead of fresh?

You can, but the flavor profile changes significantly. Dried herbs are more concentrated and lack the bright, "green" taste of fresh herbs. If using dried, reduce the quantity by half and let the butter sit for 30 minutes before using to allow the herbs to rehydrate in the fat.

How do I stop my herb butter from separating?

Separation usually happens if the butter is too hot or if the herbs are too wet. Ensure your butter is softened but not melted, and pat your fresh herbs dry with a paper towel before snipping them with your Herb Scissors.

Can I make this dairy-free?

Yes. You can substitute the dairy butter with a high-quality vegan butter stick or a chilled coconut oil base. The process remains exactly the same, though you may find that coconut oil requires a bit more stirring to incorporate the herbs evenly.
